planting.note: Set out nursery-raised saplings after all danger of frost in deep, well-drained soil; seed is notoriously slow and uneven to germinate, so scarifying or soaking seed before sowing improves odds.

directions: This massive savanna tree from sub-Saharan Africa is a wild relative of the cultivated persimmons and bears small, round, yellow-green fruit that ripens to a sweet, date-like pulp relished by wildlife and people alike. It needs a long frost-free season and deep soil to develop its characteristic buttressed trunk and broad shade canopy, and young trees grow slowly for the first several years before accelerating. Give it full sun and occasional deep watering during establishment, then step back, since mature trees are quite drought-tolerant. The dense, near-black heartwood is also prized for carving, so expect this species to be grown as much for timber and shade as for fruit.

planting.note: Transplant young trees into well-drained, even poor or stony soil during the warm season, since this species is adapted to dry deciduous forest and resents waterlogging.

directions: Native to the dry deciduous forests of the Indian subcontinent, this tough ebony relative is best known for its broad leaves, which are harvested and dried for wrapping bidi cigarettes, a major rural cottage industry across central India. The small orange fruit is edible once fully softened and ripe, though it is astringent and inedible while still firm, much like an unripe persimmon. It is markedly drought-hardy once established, tolerating poor lateritic or rocky soils and long dry seasons that would stress most fruiting trees. Full sun and minimal supplemental water suit it best, and it sheds its leaves in the dry season as a natural drought response.

planting.note: Plant in consistently moist, rich soil near water features or low-lying ground, mimicking the riverbank and swamp-forest habitat this species favors in the wild.

directions: This large tree of South and Southeast Asian riverbanks and swamp forests produces big, orange-fleshed berries whose astringent tannin-rich juice was traditionally used to dye and preserve fishing nets and leather, giving it a very different role than its sweet persimmon cousins. It wants far more moisture than most Diospyros species, thriving with its roots near permanently damp or periodically flooded ground. The pale, fine-grained heartwood, marketed as pale moon ebony, is valued for furniture and turning, so the tree is often grown as much for timber potential as for its fruit. Full sun and generous, steady watering produce the fastest growth.
sources: Forest Research Institute, India - timber species records

planting.note: Pot up collected trunk sections or nursery starts in fast-draining, mineral-heavy soil and keep nearly dry through the dormant season, since this species stores water in a swollen base and rots easily if kept wet.

directions: Native to the dry deciduous forests of Thailand and Cambodia, this small ebony relative is prized in the bonsai and pre-bonsai trade for its mottled, peeling orange-brown and gray bark and its ability to develop a thick, swollen caudex that stores water through long dry seasons. It is deciduous, dropping its leaves during drought or cool weather, then flushing back quickly once conditions improve. Grow it in a lean, sharply drained substrate in full sun, watering only once the root zone has dried, since overwatering is the most common cause of failure in cultivation. Small white flowers give way to small fruit, but the species is grown almost entirely for form and bark rather than for its fruit.

subcategory: historic dye and medicinal herb (toxic, ornamental use only)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or starts in spring in an out-of-the-way border, since this spreading herbaceous perennial can colonize ground aggressively and is grown as a historic curiosity rather than a food crop.

directions: Unlike its woody relatives, dwarf elder is entirely herbaceous, dying back to the ground each winter and resprouting from spreading rhizomes in spring, which lets it colonize hedgerows and waste ground quickly across its native European and western Asian range. The foliage has a distinctly unpleasant smell when bruised, and importantly, every part of the plant including the black autumn berries is toxic if eaten raw, so it should be grown strictly as an ornamental or historical hedgerow planting rather than harvested for food. It tolerates poor soil and some shade but spreads fastest in full sun with regular moisture, so site it where its rhizomes can be contained or where naturalizing is welcome. Cut the dead stems back hard in late fall or early spring to tidy the planting before new growth emerges.
